bet.text: Load from any angle: the turret stays pointed at the goal the entire match, so the robot can intake a note, come back and shoot immediately.

demand.text: At the reveal the robot scored in the speaker; its amp and climb plans had unresolved issues and would come at later events, and no trap function was designed in unless shooting from the ground worked.
CAD release slipped over a week, which with the complex design left too little time to fix every issue before the first event.

cycle.text: The under-bumper intake takes a note, four rollers on the turret pull it to the center at any turret angle, and the shooter takes it up with the turret already aimed. The robot also passes notes, added as another superstructure state.
One Newton attendee says it only began passing about halfway through qualifications there.

endgame.text: A light, simple climber, done at the end of the season, uses a worm gear to prevent back drive.

fallback.text: When no speaker tag is in view, the code aims the turret from the robot's pose, which is reset from the field tags the camera sees.

gave_up.text: Posters weighing 254's Newton pick say it could not score the trap, its amp was slower and less certain, and its championship auto was not adaptive; others call it the better passer.
A 254 member calls it probably the best passer at its best, but names qualification issues, little stick time and 294's defense in Newton match 11.
One poster says 1323 stole many of its Newton finals passes.

changed.text: A mid-season shooter added an amp mechanism, was more accurate, longer-ranged and nearly 10 pounds lighter, and no longer carried the climber.
The climber came at the end of the season.
Two identical robots were intended; the second was never more than a partial chassis because the team was behind schedule.
For the championship, drive gearing went from L3+ to L2+ for passing and cleanup.

outcome.text: 50-16-1 in official play; finalist in the Newton division; ranked 4 of the pooled top 20 (OPR 58.71, Newton).

solves.text: Make room for the note to enter without making the robot taller

facts.text: Narrow swerve modules from SDS; their standoffs form part of the cage that guides the note
The front modules are in a narrow configuration so the note passes between them instead of over the top
Production sample MK4n modules
It is modeled after the Spectrum intake and takes notes from all kinds of angles
Rollers use black silicone from McMaster, the same material as the year before
Electrical tape over the silicone of the rearmost intake roller, for less grip at the same thickness, stopped notes escaping out the top
Teflon tape on the surface opposite the rollers, and on the decks and wire tunnel, helps notes slide
Two Krakens drive the whole S-path for power; the upper and lower parts were first powered separately
Roller hubs are epoxied into plastic tubes, with the pulleys lined up before it sets
Roller pulleys and end caps are printed in Onyx

cost.text: Notes could get stuck on the way into the teacup rollers; grip mattered, so rollers were wiped with baby wipes before every match and at each battery change on the practice field
Tread wear let the lower roller rub the ground, which burned out the lower intake motor
Some printed Onyx roller ends failed, always after some other event such as a drop

functions.name: Load-from-any-angle feed

solves.text: Feed the shooter whatever direction the turret is pointing

functions.type: four vertical rollers on the turret

facts.text: A note that touches the rollers at any angle is pulled around the turret and to the center, then taken up by the shooter
It is like the 254 spindexer with two entry points, so the note enters through the 180-degree arc facing the intake
The side of the turret that receives the note switches as the shooter passes 90 degrees
The motor-driven teacup rollers turn the note whichever way is shorter to the feeder
Teacups are driven coaxially through the turret center with belts; horizontal rollers and belts then lift the note to the shooter
One printed coaxial spool, with six dowel pins pressed in for strength, drives the two sides in opposite directions
Three layers of silicone on both end sections of two rollers give more compression to get the note through the S-bend
Prototypes checked the worst-case turret angles; no other feeder concept was tested

cost.text: Feeding takes slightly longer with the turret at 90 or 270 degrees, because the 'teacup' rollers touch the note as it enters
Getting the note through the S-bend draws significant power

solves.text: Be aimed before the robot arrives, with the stage or other robots in the way

facts.text: Range either side of center
Tracks the speaker continuously in teleop
Two sheathed wire bundles come up through the center and spiral on a flat plate over that range
One X-contact bearing, equivalent to a Kaydon KC090XP0, carries it: outer race clamped to the turret, inner race to the base
The bearing never gave issues; extras were bought as a precaution
A 70T gear on the turret drives a 36T encoder gear that drives a 34T one, so two absolute encoders find the angle at startup across all turns
The angle comes from the team's own algorithm, not the Chinese remainder theorem
Turret chain tension is set by bolting an eccentric part through a different set of holes
Shooting spins up the flywheels, feeds the note and points the turret at the goal
A later version was nearly 10 pounds lighter with greater range and accuracy
In the later version the left and right wheels still run at different speeds, turning independently on a shared dead axle
Solid 60A urethane wheels, small for packaging and geared to match the surface speed of successful 3 and 4 in designs; diameter
The printed Onyx wheel hub press fit was loose, so it was epoxied
The released CAD shows the wrong shooter belt; the robot uses a double-sided belt of
A waterjet-cut configurable prototype vibrated at higher speeds; most of the final geometry came from 6328's and 111's open designs

cost.text: The first version carried the climber, so it needed a lot of structure and gear reduction

solves.text: Score the amp with the shooter without the note falling back out

facts.text: The shooter fires the note straight up and the bar keeps it from falling out
The team says the amp part had to be light
Light and simple, with a worm gear to prevent back drive

cost.text: The design put high load on the climber motor: it stalled after early successes, then drew about 180 amps after a firmware rollback; one motor burned out at the district championship even though the team e-stopped right after climbing. No root cause was found and the team recommends other designs

solves.text: Keep the turret on the goal when the tag is hidden

facts.text: With a speaker tag in view, the turret set point is moved to drive the horizontal error to zero
Without one, the robot's pose gives a field-relative turret angle, converted to robot-relative from the drive heading
Field tags reset odometry, with the robot pose calculated for where the rotating camera sits
A Limelight 3 under the shooter

cost.text: A camera that rotates on the turret made the pose calculation a problem the team had to work through

solves.text: Avoid several interdependent commands per button

facts.text: A button pushes one super-state, and the superstructure pushes sub-states to each subsystem
The class extends the WPILib subsystem base, so it makes state transitions periodically
Height with the shooter down, about
The reveal post calls it the team's shortest robot yet

decisions.choice: Prototype the roller feed before designing the robot
decisions.because: the team did not know whether rollers at the center could pull a note to the middle

decisions.choice: One superstructure class that pushes states
decisions.because: it keeps the code clean and makes features such as passing easy to add
decisions.instead_of: buttons that each run several interdependent commands

decisions.choice: Use the shooter and a light bar for the amp
decisions.because: the amp part had to be light

decisions.choice: Worm gear on a light, simple climber
decisions.because: the climber was done at the end of the season and had to resist back drive
pivot motors in brake could not hold the robot up long enough, the hook sat too far from the center of gravity and hung it too steeply, and the turret brake could not stop the base turning
decisions.instead_of: a spring-powered polycarbonate hook released by a solenoid, with the shooter pivot pulling down

decisions.because: the robot is power hungry; with the same current limits L2+ gives more torque and response against defense on passing and in cleanup

decisions.choice: Validate concepts with limited prototypes, then build the final design
decisions.because: shop space is short and manufacturing sponsors are strong, so building and then adjusting is more efficient
the build was behind schedule, parts were complex, many were machined, and the design would keep changing; work on one robot taught the team faster
decisions.instead_of: the intended second, identical robot, stopped about a third of the way through assembly

decisions.choice: Fly the robot to the championship as checked luggage
decisions.because: it gives about five more days of work than shipping, and many improvements were made in those days
decisions.cost: the base is overweight and oversize luggage, and must stay under the airline limit of 100 pounds; the turret travels separately
